The Duke said:
"Excellent!
I asked about governance,
and you instructed me on matters of education."
Zǐ said:
"The ruler asked about the method of cān參, referencing the regulations of the Yellow Emperor (Huángdì),
the grand rituals of regulation."
The Duke said:
"Is the Way of the former sages
to be considered beautiful?"
Zǐ said:
"It is to be considered beautiful.
Even if there is beauty,
it must be one-sided.
If it belongs to this (the Way),
it illuminates the blessings of Heaven,
and is greeted with auspiciousness;
it creates the blessings of Earth,
and is regulated with prosperity;
it elevates the virtue of the people,
and is guarded with longevity."
The Duke said:
"Excellent!"

"Principal Words, 39th"
*Kǒngzǐ* was at leisure,
*Zēngzǐ* was in attendance.
*Kǒngzǐ* said:
"*Shēn*!
The gentlemen of today
only hear the words of scholars and high officials;
as for the words of a true gentleman,
they are very rare.
Alas!
Will my principal words not be uttered and I die?
How sad!"
*Zēngzǐ* rose and said:
"May I venture to ask what are principal words?"
*Kǒngzǐ* did not answer.
*Zēngzǐ* was afraid,
solemnly gathered his clothes and descended from the mat,
saying:
"Your disciple knows it is disrespectful.
It is difficult to have a moment of leisure with you, Master,
therefore I dared to ask."
*Kǒngzǐ* did not answer.
*Zēngzǐ* was afraid,
and retreated, leaning against the west wall and standing there.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Cān!
Can I discuss the Dao of an enlightened ruler with you?"
Zēngzǐ said:
"I dare not consider myself sufficient.
It is difficult to find leisure with you, Master,
therefore I dare to ask."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"I will tell you.
Dao [道],
is that by which virtue is made manifest;
virtue [德],
is that by which Dao is honored.
Therefore, without virtue, Dao is not honored;
without Dao, virtue is not made manifest.
Even if one has excellent horses in the state,
if they are not trained, they will not obey,
and you cannot travel a thousand *lǐ*.
Even if one has vast lands and many people,
if one does not govern them according to its Dao,
one cannot become a paramount ruler.
Therefore, in the past, enlightened rulers cultivated the Seven Teachings internally,
and practiced the Three Reaches externally.
If the Seven Teachings are cultivated,
one can defend;
if the Three Reaches are practiced,
How can one conquer?
If the Seven Teachings are not cultivated,
even defense will not be secure;
if the Three Visits are not implemented,
even conquest will not bring submission.
Therefore, the defense of an enlightened ruler
must break the enemy's advance thousands of *lǐ* away;
and their conquests
result in the return of the army from the sleeping mats.
Therefore, cultivating the Seven Teachings internally ensures the ruler is not burdened,
and implementing the Three Visits externally ensures wealth is not wasted.
This is what is called the way of an enlightened ruler."
Zēng Zǐ said:
"May I ask, can not wasting and not being burdened be considered enlightenment?"
Kǒngzǐ looked grave, raised his eyebrows, and said:
"Cān!
Do you consider an enlightened ruler to be burdened?
In the past, Shùn had Yǔ on his left and Gāo Yáo on his right,
and without leaving his mat, the world was governed.
If the administration is not aligned with the Way,
it is the ruler's fault.
If the administration is aligned with the Way,
and yet the commands are not followed,
it is the fault of those in charge of duties.
Why would an enlightened ruler be burdened!
In the past, an enlightened ruler supervised border crossings but did not levy taxes,
managed the markets but did not collect duties,
To tax at a rate of one tenth;
to employ the people's labor no more than three days per year;
to enter the mountains and marshes at the proper times;
to have prohibitions but no levies:
these six are the ways to obtain wealth.
An enlightened ruler abandons four of these and moderates the remaining two.
From where, then, does an enlightened ruler obtain his expenses!"
Zēngzǐ said:
"May I ask, what are the Seven Teachings?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"When superiors respect the elderly, then inferiors will increasingly show filial piety.
When superiors honor age, then inferiors will increasingly show fraternal respect.
When superiors delight in bestowing favors, then inferiors will increasingly show trustworthiness.
When superiors are close to the virtuous, then inferiors will select their friends carefully.
When superiors cherish virtue, then inferiors will not conceal their faults.
When superiors detest greed, then inferiors will be ashamed to contend.
When superiors are steadfast and resolute, then inferiors will value integrity and a sense of shame.
When the people all have distinctions, then they will be upright,
and correcting them will not be difficult.
These are called the Seven Teachings.
The Seven Teachings
are the foundation for governing the people.
Once the teachings are established, then all is rectified.
Superiors
are the standard for the people.
If the standard is correct, then what could be incorrect?
Therefore, if the ruler first establishes himself in benevolence,
Then the senior officials are loyal and the scholars trustworthy,
the people are honest and the artisans simple,
the merchants are sincere and the women innocent,
wives are selfless,
these seven,
are the aims of education.
These seven,
spread throughout the world and the four directions without being excessive,
contained within ordinary rooms without being obstructed.
Therefore, the sage regulates them with ritual propriety,
establishes them with righteousness,
conducts them with obedience,
and the people's rejection of evil is like washing."
Zēngzǐ said:
"As for disciples, I am insufficient,
but the Dao is perfect."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Shēn!
Please stop,
there is more.
In the past, enlightened rulers had methods for governing the people,
they necessarily divided the land into provinces,
assigned them to different jurisdictions to govern,
so that virtuous people had nowhere to hide,
and violent people had nowhere to lurk.
They made officials inspect them daily and examine them periodically,
encouraging virtue annually,
Then the virtuous are drawn near,
and the unworthy are put in fear.
He causes them to grieve for widowers and widows,
to support orphans and the lonely,
to relieve the poor,
to encourage filial piety and brotherly respect,
and to select the virtuous and promote the capable.
If these seven are cultivated,
then within the four seas there will be no criminal people.
If the ruler's closeness to his subjects is like his own belly and heart,
then the subjects' closeness to the ruler will be like a child seeing its loving mother.
When the closeness between ruler and subjects is like this,
then orders are followed,
and decrees are carried out.
Relying on the people who are near, they are persuaded and submit;
those who are far away come and are drawn in.
Then, using the finger to know the inch,
using the hand to know the foot,
extending the elbow to know the fathom,
using ten fathoms for a *suǒ* (rope).
One hundred paces for a wall (*dǔ*),
three hundred paces for a *lǐ* (neighborhood),
one thousand paces for a well,
three wells for a *jùliè* (district),
three *jùliè* for a *jù* (larger district),
fifty *lǐ* for a border (*fēng*),
and one hundred *lǐ* for a capital city.
Thereupon stores of clothing and furs are accumulated,
Those who stay behind care for those who travel, sharing what they have or lack.
Therefore, the Mányí 蠻夷 barbarians and the various Xià 夏 peoples,
though their clothing and customs are different,
and their languages do not match,
all come
to pay homage to the king.
Therefore it is said:
"Without markets, the people lack nothing;
without punishments, the people do not disobey."
The gains from hunting with nets and arrows,
are not used to fill the palaces and chambers;
the taxes collected from the common people
are not used to fill the treasuries.
[He] sympathizes to make up for deficiencies,
and uses propriety to reduce excesses.
Therefore it is said: "Much sincerity, but few outward displays."
His rituals are worthy of being followed,
his words are worthy of being repeated,
and his actions are worthy of being emulated.
His faithfulness
is like the four seasons of spring, autumn, winter, and summer;
his broad benevolence towards the myriad people
is like food for the hungry,
and drink for the thirsty.
The people of the lower realms trust him!
Heat, cold, freezing, and warmth,
those far away become like those near;
it's not the Way that is near,
and their illustrious virtue.
Therefore, without moving soldiers or weapons, they possess authority;
without bestowing benefits, they gain affection.
This is what is meant by the defense of an enlightened ruler.
Deflecting attacks from beyond a thousand *lǐ*,
this is what is meant."
Zēngzǐ said:
"May I venture to ask, what are the Three Perfections?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Perfect propriety requires no concession, and the world is governed;
perfect reward costs nothing, and the scholars of the world are pleased;
perfect music is soundless, and the people of the world are harmonious.
An enlightened ruler sincerely practices the Three Perfections;
therefore, the rulers of the world can be understood,
the scholars of the world can be made his ministers,
and the people of the world can be employed."
Zēngzǐ said:
"May I venture to ask, what is meant by this?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"In the past, enlightened kings invariably knew the names of all the worthy men in the world;
having known their names,
they also knew their number;
having known their number,
they also knew their location.
An enlightened ruler elevates the scholars of the world by means of the ranks available in the world;
this is what is meant by 'perfect propriety requires no concession, and the world is governed.'
Using the emoluments of the empire to enrich the scholars of the empire,
this is called supreme reward that does not expend resources, yet the scholars of the empire are pleased.
When the scholars of the empire are pleased,
then the most brilliant reputations in the empire will arise.
This is called supreme joy that is without sound, yet the people of the empire are harmonious.
Therefore, it is said:
That which is called the ultimate benevolence in the empire
is the ability to unite those who are closest in the empire.
That which is called the ultimate wisdom in the empire
is the ability to employ those who are most harmonious in the empire.
That which is called the ultimate clarity in the empire
is the ability to select those who are most virtuous in the empire.
When these three are all interconnected,
then one can launch a military campaign.
Therefore, for the benevolent, nothing is greater than loving people;
for the wise, nothing is greater than knowing the worthy;
for the ruler, nothing is greater than employing the worthy.
If a ruler of a territory cultivates these three,
then those within the four seas will respectfully await his arrival,
and then he can launch a military campaign.
What a wise ruler campaigns against
is that which has abandoned the Dao.
They abandon the Dao and do not practice it,
then punish their ruler,
carry out the campaign,
console their people, and do not seize their wealth.
Therefore, it is said:
The campaign of a wise ruler
It is like timely rain;
when it arrives, the people rejoice.
Therefore, if one's generosity is extensive
and one gains the affection of the multitude,
this is what is meant by "returning the army upon the mat."
*Āi Gōng* Asked About the Five Virtues, Section Forty.
*Lǔ Āi Gōng* asked *Kǒngzǐ* saying:
"I wish to assess the gentlemen of my state
and govern with them.
What kind should I choose?"
*Kǒngzǐ* replied,
"Living in the present age,
aspiring to the ways of antiquity,
dwelling amidst contemporary customs,
wearing the garments of antiquity,
those who abandon this to do what is wrong,
are they not rare indeed!"
*Āi Gōng* said,
"Then are all those who wear a tall cap (*zhāngfǔ*), curved shoes (*gōujú*), silk belt (*shēndài*), and hold a tablet (*jìnhù*)
all virtuous?"
*Kǒngzǐ* said,
"No!
Not necessarily.
Now, those who wear formal attire (*duān yī*), black lower garment (*xuán cháng*), a crown (*miǎn*), and ride in a grand carriage (*lù*),
their minds may not be focused on eating meat; those who wear mourning garments (*zhǎncuī*), rush shoes (*jiānjù*), carry a staff and sip congee,
their minds may not be focused on food and drink.
Therefore, to live in the present age,
aspire to the ways of the ancients,
reside in the customs of the present,
and wear the clothes of the ancients,
abandoning this to pursue something else,
even if there are such people,
would they not be rare indeed!"
Āi Gōng said,
"Excellent!
What kind of person can be called a mediocre person?"
Kǒngzǐ replied,
"Those who are called mediocre people,
their mouths cannot speak good words,
and their hearts are not anxious;
they cannot choose virtuous and capable men and entrust themselves to them,
taking their concerns as their own;
in action, they do not know what to pursue,
in stillness, they do not know where to settle;
daily selecting from things,
they do not know what is valuable;
flowing with things,
they do not know where to return;
the five senses used for governing,
the mind decays accordingly.
Such a person,
can be called a mediocre person."
Duke Āi said:
"Excellent!
What must one do to be called a *shì* (士)?"
Kǒngzǐ replied:
"Those called *shì* (士),
though they may not fully comprehend the Way and its techniques,
must have something to adhere to;
though they may not fully attain perfect goodness and beauty,
must have something to dwell in.
Therefore, in knowledge, they do not strive for quantity,
but strive to carefully examine what they know;
in action, they do not strive for quantity,
but strive to carefully examine what they follow;
in speech, they do not strive for quantity,
but strive to carefully examine what they say.
When they know something, they truly know it;
when they act, they truly follow it;
when they speak, they truly agree with it,
like the inherent nature of one's life, destiny, flesh, and skin, which cannot be changed.
Wealth and high position cannot increase it,
poverty and low position cannot diminish it.
If one is like this,
then one can be called a *shì* (士)."
Duke Āi said:
"Excellent!
What must one do to be called a *jūnzǐ* (君子)?"
Kǒngzǐ replied:
"The so-called *jūnzǐ*
personally practices loyalty and trustworthiness,
and their heart is not lacking in virtue.
*Rén* and *yì* reside within them,
yet they are not harmed by what they do not know.
They hear of vast and extensive aspirations, yet their countenance does not boast.
Their thoughts and deliberations are clear and insightful, yet their words are not contentious.
They seem as if they can be reached,
yet cannot be reached.
One who is like this,
can be called a *jūnzǐ*."
Āi Gōng said:
"Excellent!
May I venture to ask, what qualities define a *xiánrén*?"
Kǒngzǐ replied:
"The so-called *xiánrén*
shares the same feelings of likes and dislikes with the people,
and the same principles of acceptance and rejection with the people.
Their actions adhere to the compass and straightedge,
yet do not harm the foundation.
Their words are sufficient to set an example for the world,
yet do not harm themselves.
Though in person a commoner, they wish for wealth,
though noble as a *zhūhóu*, they are without riches.
One who is like this,
can be called a *xiánrén*."
Duke Āi said:
"Excellent!
May I venture to ask, how can one be called a sage?"
Kǒngzǐ replied:
"Those who are called sages
understand and are thoroughly versed in the Great Dao,
respond to changes without exhaustion,
and can fathom the feelings and natures of all things.
The Great Dao
is that by which transformations occur and all things are formed and solidified.
Feelings and natures
are that by which things are naturally ordered, without selection or rejection.
Therefore, their affairs are great,
matching Heaven and Earth,
participating with the sun and moon,
mingling with the clouds and rainbows,
encompassing and summarizing all things.
Deep and pure,
none can follow their path,
like the controller of Heaven;
none can hold their office,
the common people are indifferent and do not know their goodness.
If one is like this,
then one can be called a sage."
Duke Āi said:
"Excellent."
Kǒngzǐ departed,
Āi Gōng saw him off.
"Āi Gōng Asks Confucius, Chapter Forty-One"
Āi Gōng asked Confucius, saying:
"What are the great Rites like?
When gentlemen speak of Rites,
why do they esteem them so highly?"
Confucius said:
"Qiū is a man of little account;
how could I possibly know about the Rites?"
The lord said:
"No,
please, Master, tell me about them."
Confucius said:
"I have heard it said that,
of that by which the people live,
the Rites are the greatest.
Without the Rites, there is no way to regulate the service to the gods of Heaven and Earth.
Without the Rites, there is no way to distinguish the positions of ruler and subject, superior and inferior, elder and younger.
Without the Rites, there is no way to differentiate the affections of men and women, father and son, brothers, the closeness of marriage, and the degrees of intimacy in social interactions.
This is why the gentleman esteems them.
Then, with what he is capable of, he teaches the common people,
not abandoning their gatherings and festivals;
when there is a completed undertaking,
then he attends to its carvings and engravings, its ornamentation of embroidered axes and patterned silks, so as to perpetuate it;
when they are in order,
then he speaks of the regulations for funerals,
prepares the cauldrons and sacrificial vessels,
If they prepare the dried meat for the winter sacrifice,
and renovate their ancestral temples,
reverently offering sacrifices at the proper times of the year,
and maintain order within the lineage,
then they should secure their dwellings,
make plain their clothing,
keep their palaces humble,
not carve intricate designs on their carriages,
not engrave elaborate patterns on their utensils,
not eat more than one kind of meat at a meal,
and share the benefits with the people.
This is how the gentlemen of the past practiced ritual."
The Duke said,
"Why do none of the gentlemen of today
practice these things?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"The gentlemen of today
are insatiable in their love of beauty,
tireless in their pursuit of excessive virtue,
wastefully idle and arrogant,
certainly exhausting the people,
opposing the masses to attack those who possess the Dao,
seeking to obtain what they desire improperly.
In the past, those who employed the people led from the front;
today, those who employ the people lag behind.
The gentlemen of today do not practice ritual."
Kǒngzǐ was attending Āi Gōng.
Āi Gōng said:
"May I venture to ask, what is the greatest of human principles?"
Kǒngzǐ looked grave and changed his expression, replying:
"That Your Lordship should touch upon such a matter,
is a blessing for the common people.
Indeed, your servant dares not decline to answer.
Of human principles, governance is the greatest."
The Duke said:
"May I venture to ask, what is meant by 'governance'?"
Kǒngzǐ replied:
"Governance means
correctness.
If the ruler is correct,
then the common people will follow governance.
What the ruler does,
the common people will follow.
What the ruler does not do,
what will the common people follow?"
The Duke said:
"May I venture to ask, how is governance to be carried out?"
Kǒngzǐ replied:
"Let husband and wife be distinct,
father and son be close,
ruler and subject be respectful;
if these three are correct,
Then the common people will follow him."
The Duke said:
"Although I, the unworthy one, am not like them,
I would like to hear how to implement the way of these three words.
Is it possible for me to hear it?"
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) replied:
"In ancient times, governing
loving the people was the greatest thing.
The means to govern and love the people
ritual was the greatest;
the means to govern ritual,
reverence was the greatest;
the utmost of reverence
the Great Marriage was the greatest.
The Great Marriage is utmost!
When the Great Marriage arrives,
to wear the crown and personally greet the bride,
is to show intimacy.
To show intimacy,
is to show intimacy.
Therefore, the superior man cultivates reverence to show intimacy,
abandoning reverence is to abandon intimacy.
Without love, there is no intimacy;
without reverence, there is no correctness.
Love and reverence, are the root of governance!"
The Duke said:
"I, the widowed one, wish to speak.
To wear the ceremonial cap and personally welcome the bride,
isn't that exceedingly important?"
Kǒngzǐ looked stern and changed his expression, replying:
"To unite the bond of two surnames,
to continue the posterity of the former sages,
to establish the lord of Heaven and Earth, the Altars of the Soil and Grain, and the ancestral temple,
why does Your Lordship consider it exceedingly important?"
The Duke said:
"I am indeed stubborn.
If I were not stubborn,
how could I have heard these words?
I wished to ask,
but could not find the words,
please, let me inquire further."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"If Heaven and Earth do not harmonize,
the myriad things will not be born.
The great marriage
is the succession for ten thousand generations;
how can Your Lordship consider it exceedingly important?"
Thereupon Kǒngzǐ spoke, saying:
"Inwardly, it governs the rites of the ancestral temple,
sufficient to be paired with the spirits of Heaven and Earth;
outwardly, it governs the rites of straightforward speech,
sufficient to establish respect between superiors and inferiors.
Shame over personal matters is enough to rouse one;
shame over national matters is enough to revitalize the nation.
Governing begins with propriety.
Propriety,
is it not the foundation of government!"
Kǒngzǐ then said:
"In the past, the government of the enlightened kings of the Three Dynasties
certainly respected their wives and children;
there was reason for this.
A wife,
she is the master of the household,
how dare one not respect her?
A son,
he is the continuation of the parents,
how dare one not respect him?
A junzi has nothing that he does not respect,
and respecting oneself is the greatest.
One's self,
it is a branch of one's parents,
how dare one not respect it?
If one cannot respect one's self,
it is to harm one's parents;
harming one's parents,
is to harm the root;
harming the root,
the branches will accordingly perish.
These three
This is the image of the common people.
Regarding oneself as well as one's body,
one's children as well as one's children,
one's spouse as well as one's spouse.
If the *jūnzǐ* (君子) practices these three,
then he will inspire the whole world.
This is the way of the great king.
If it is like this,
the state will be harmonious."
The Duke said:
"May I ask what is meant by respecting oneself?"
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) replied:
"If the *jūnzǐ* (君子) speaks excessively, then the people will create rhetoric;
if he acts excessively, then the people will create standards.
If the *jūnzǐ* (君子)'s words do not exceed rhetoric,
and his actions do not exceed standards,
the people will be respectful and reverent without being ordered to do so.
If it is like this,
then he can respect himself.
If he can respect himself,
then he can bring about the success of his parents."
The Duke said:
"May I ask what is meant by bringing about the success of one's parents?"
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) replied:
"The *jūnzǐ* (君子) is
a person who achieves fame.
When the common people submit to him, his reputation
is called "the son of a *jūnzǐ*,"
thus causing his parents to be *jūnzǐ* too.
This is to complete the reputation of his parents."
Kǒngzǐ then said:
"In ancient times, when people governed,
loving the people was paramount.
If you cannot love the people,
you cannot possess yourself;
if you cannot possess yourself,
you cannot secure the land;
if you cannot secure the land,
you cannot find joy in Heaven;
if you cannot find joy in Heaven,
you cannot perfect yourself."
The Duke said:
"May I ask what you mean by 'perfecting oneself'?"
Kǒngzǐ replied:
"Not being overcome by external things."
The Duke said:
"May I ask what you value in the Way of Heaven?"
Kǒngzǐ replied:
"I value its ceaselessness.
Like the sun and moon following each other from west to east without end,
this is the Way of Heaven.
Not closing for a long time,
this is the Way of Heaven.
Accomplishing things through inaction,
this is the Way of Heaven.
Becoming complete and being enlightened,
this is the Way of Heaven."
Gōng (公) said:
"I, your subject, am foolish, ignorant, and deeply troubled.
You understand my heart."
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) quickly stood up from his mat and replied:
"The benevolent person does not go beyond things,
the filial son does not go beyond things.
Therefore, the benevolent person's serving of parents is like serving Heaven;
serving Heaven is like serving parents.
Therefore, the filial son completes himself."
Gōng (公) said:
"Now that I have heard these words,
what can be done about my past offenses?"
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) replied:
"Your Majesty's consideration of these words
is this servant's good fortune."
*The Three Roots of Rites*, Forty-second Chapter
Rites have three roots:
Heaven and Earth,
are the root of nature;
Ancestors are the
root of one's lineage;
rulers and teachers are the
root of governance.
Without Heaven and Earth, where would life originate?
Without ancestors, from where would one emerge?
Without rulers and teachers, how would there be order?
If any of these three are missing,
there will be no peace for the people.
Therefore, in ritual,
one serves Heaven above,
serves Earth below,
honors ancestors, and favors rulers and teachers;
these are the three roots of ritual.
The king takes Heaven as the great ancestor;
the feudal lords dare not presume to do so.
High officials and officers have their established ancestral temples;
this is how to distinguish nobility at the origin,
the root of virtue.
Sacrifices at the suburban altar (jiāo) are limited to the Son of Heaven;
sacrifices at the state altar (shè) are limited to the feudal lords;
principles extend to high officials and officers;
this is how to distinguish the honored and the lowly.
The honored serve the honored,
the lowly serve the lowly,
what is fitting in great matters is handled greatly,
what is fitting in small matters is handled small.
Therefore, those who possess the empire serve for seven generations;
those who possess a state serve for five generations;
those who possess a land with five chariots serve for three generations;
those who possess a land with three chariots serve for two generations;
those who wait until old age to eat are not allowed to establish ancestral temples.
This is how one distinguishes that those who have accumulated wealth deeply have abundant and illustrious blessings,
and those who have accumulated wealth meagerly have lowly and insignificant blessings. This is also true.
In the great banquet, the xuán zūn (玄尊, dark-colored sacrificial vessel) is valued,
and the zu (俎, sacrificial stand) presents raw fish.
The dà gēng (大羹, thick broth) is served first,
valuing the origins of food and drink.
In the great banquet, the xuán zūn (玄尊, dark-colored sacrificial vessel) is valued and wine is used,
sorghum and millet are eaten before rice and millet,
the dà gēng (大羹, thick broth) is tasted in the sacrifice and one is sated with various delicacies,
valuing the origin and being close to practical use.
Valuing the origin is called wén (文, culture),
being close to practical use is called lǐ (理, principle),
the two combined create wén (文, culture),

*The Virtue of the Five Emperors*, Sixty-Second
Zǎi Wǒ asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"In the past, I heard from Róng Yīlìng
that the Yellow Emperor ruled for three hundred years.
May I ask, was the Yellow Emperor a man?
Or was he not a man?
How did he live for three hundred years?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Yǔ!
Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, Wǔ, Chéng Wáng, Zhōu Gōng—can they be fully comprehended?
The Huángdì is too lofty to discuss.
What is it you intend to do?

Zǎi Wǒ said:
"The traditions of ancient times,
the obscure and subtle accounts,
the fully concluded arguments,
and the vague and neglected meanings are
not the way of the superior man.
Therefore, my questions are well-founded."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The Huángdì
was the son of Shǎodiǎn,
known as Xuānyuán.
He was born with a divine spirit,
could speak when he was still weak,
was intelligent and orderly as a child,
was honest and quick-witted when he grew up,
and was discerning and wise when he came of age.
He regulated the five *qì*,
established the five measures,
comforted the myriad people,
surveyed the four directions,
and taught bears, grizzlies, *pí*, leopards, and tigers,
and fought with the Chìdì (赤帝) in the fields of Bǎnquán (版泉).
After three battles,
he was then able to carry out his ambitions.
The Huángdì (黃帝) wore embroidered ceremonial robes,
a large belt,
and an embroidered skirt.
He rode a dragon-drawn carriage adorned with clouds,
in order to follow the laws of heaven and earth,
the reasons for darkness and light,
the doctrines of life and death,
and the difficulties of existence and extinction.
He then sowed the various grains and plants.
Therefore, he civilized and transformed the birds, beasts, insects, and creatures.
He calculated the movements of the sun, moon, and stars.
He exhausted the produce of the soil, stones, metals, and jades.
He taxed his heart, strength, ears, and eyes.
He economized in the use of water, fire, and materials.
While alive, the people benefited from him for a hundred years.
After his death, the people revered his spirit for a hundred years.
After his demise, the people used his teachings for a hundred years.
Therefore, it is said, 'Three hundred years.'"
Zǎi Wǒ (宰我) asked about the Dì Zhuānxū (帝顓頊).
Confucius said,
"The Five Emperors used records,
the Three Kings used measures.
You want to understand the accounts of the ancient past in a single day?
How rash you are, Yǔ (予)!"
Zǎi Wǒ
said:
"In the past,
'Young men should not have lingering questions.'"

"Zhuānxū,
grandson of the Huángdì,
son of Chāngyì,
was called Gāoyáng.
He was profound and resourceful,
knowledgeable in dredging and communication,
nurtured talent to suit the land,
followed the seasons to emulate Heaven,
relied on ghosts and spirits to establish righteousness,
regulated the vital energy to instruct the people,

Riding a dragon, he reached the four seas,
north to Yōulíng,
south to Jiāozhǐ,
west across the quicksand,

He was born with spiritual intelligence

He generously bestowed benefits on all things,

*Exhortation to Learning*, Section Sixty-Four
The gentleman says:
Learning cannot be stopped.
Indigo blue is taken from the indigo plant,
but is bluer than the indigo plant;
water becomes ice,
and is colder than water.
Wood that is straight can be made true by a plumb line,
if bent into a wheel,
its curve will conform to a compass;
even if it dries out, it will not return to being straight,
because bending has made it so.
Therefore, without climbing a high mountain,
one does not know the height of the sky;
without looking into a deep ravine,
one does not know the thickness of the earth;
without hearing the doctrines left by the former kings,
unaware of the vastness of learning.
The children of the Gānyuè, Róng and Hé barbarians,
are born with the same voices,
but grow up with different customs;
it is education that makes them so.
Therefore, wood follows the string and becomes straight,
metal is applied to the whetstone and becomes sharp.
The superior man learns extensively and examines himself thrice daily,
therefore his knowledge is clear and his actions are without fault.
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"Ah, you gentlemen,
do not constantly seek repose.
Be respectfully attentive to your position,
and cherish what is upright.
The spirits will listen to you,
and bestow on you great blessings."
Nothing is greater than being transformed by the Dao,
and no blessing is greater than being without blame.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"I once spent the whole day thinking,
but it was not as good as a moment's learning;
I once stood on tiptoe and looked into the distance,
but it was not as good as climbing high for a broad view."
Climbing high and beckoning,
does not mean the arms are longer,
but what is seen is far;
calling with the wind,
It is not that the sound becomes louder,
but the listener perceives it as distinct.
One who uses carts and horses
does not have swift feet,
yet reaches a thousand *lǐ*;
one who uses boats and oars
is not skilled in swimming,
yet crosses rivers and seas.
The nature of the *jūnzǐ* is no different,
they are good at making use of things.
In the south there is a bird,
called *wūjiū*,
which makes its nest with feathers,
weaving them with hair,
and attaching it to reeds.
When the wind comes, the reeds break,
the young die and the eggs are broken.
It is not that the nest is not complete,
but that which it is attached to is the problem.
In the west there is a tree,
called *yègān*,
with a stem four *cùn* long,
growing on top of a high mountain,
overlooking a hundred-*rèn* deep abyss.
It is not that the stem of the tree is able to grow long,
but what it stands upon makes it so.
Hemp growing among flax
stands upright without support.

cultivates himself and focuses his will,
must choose his community carefully,

The arising of things,

dried fish breeds weevils.

The strong bring about their own downfall,
the weak bring about their own constraint.
If wickedness is in oneself,
it is the source of resentment.
If firewood is laid out evenly,
the fire goes to the dry places;
if the ground is level,
water flows to the wet places.
Plants and trees grow in rows;
birds and beasts live in groups.

Therefore, words can summon disaster,
and actions can invite disgrace.
The virtuous person is careful about where he stands.
Accumulate earth to form a mountain,
and wind and rain will arise;
accumulate water to form a river,

accumulate good deeds to cultivate virtue,
and spiritual enlightenment will naturally come,

one cannot reach a thousand *lǐ*;
without accumulating small streams,
one cannot form the great rivers and seas.

a dull horse, without limit,

Carve a little and then abandon it,

To carve without stopping,
even metal and stone can be engraved.
Now, the earthworm, without the advantage of claws or teeth,
or the strength of sinews and veins,
above eats dried earth,
below drinks from the Yellow Springs,
because it is single-minded;
the crab, with two claws and eight legs,
not inhabiting the holes of snakes or eels,
has nowhere to entrust itself,
because it is restless.
Therefore, those without a resolute ambition
have no clear understanding;
those without continuous effort
have no outstanding achievement.
Those who walk haltingly on the road will not arrive,
those who serve two lords will not be tolerated.
The eye cannot see clearly while looking in two directions,
the ear cannot hear distinctly while listening to two sounds.
The *téngshé* serpent has no feet yet soars,
the *shíshǔ* squirrel has five skills yet is impoverished.
The *Classic of Poetry* says:

its young are seven.
The virtuous gentleman,
his conduct is single.

The superior man is one who focuses on unity.
In the past,
when Hù Bā 瓠巴 played the zither, fish submerged and came out to listen;

No sound is so subtle that it cannot be heard,
and no action is so hidden that it does not manifest.
Jade dwells in the mountains, and the trees are moistened;
pearls are produced in the depths, and the banks do not dry up.
If one does good deeds without accumulating them,
how can one expect to achieve anything?
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said:
How uncultivated!
A superior man cannot but learn.
When meeting people, one cannot but adorn oneself;
without adornment, one lacks proper appearance;
without proper appearance, one lacks respect;
without respect, one lacks propriety;
without propriety, one cannot stand.
That which is far away but has light
is adornment;
that which is near but becomes increasingly bright
is learning.
It is like a stagnant pool:
floodwaters collect there,
and cattails and reeds grow there.
Viewed from above,
who would know that it is not a spring?
Pearls are the
*yīn* within *yáng*,
therefore they overcome fire.
Jade is the
*yáng* within *yīn*,
therefore it overcomes water. Their transformations are like magic.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) stores pearls and jade,
the feudal lords (zhūhóu) store gold and stone,
the high officials (dàfū) keep dogs and horses,
and the common people (bǎixìng) store cloth and silk.
If not,
then the strong will be able to guard them,
and the wise will be able to control them.
To disdain what should be valued and value what should be disdained
—if not,
the widowed, orphaned, and solitary will not obtain them.
Zǐ Gòng said:
"When a *jūnzǐ* sees a great river, he will surely observe it.
Why is this?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Water
is what a *jūnzǐ* compares his virtue to.
It bestows impartially without selfishness,
resembling virtue;
what it reaches lives,
what it does not reach dies,
resembling benevolence;
Its flowing, seeping downwards, and curving,
all follow its natural principle,
seemingly righteous;
its plunging into a hundred-ren ravine
without hesitation,
seemingly courageous;
the shallow allows for flowing,
the deep abyss is unfathomable,
seemingly wise;
it passes through weak, constricted, dangerous places,
seemingly discerning;
it accepts filth without rejecting it,
seemingly faithful;
it enters covered in uncleanliness,
and emerges pristine,
seemingly transformative;
it must come out,
and its volume must be level,
seemingly upright;
when full, it does not seek to be leveled,
seemingly strict;
when it bends, it does so necessarily in the east or west direction,
seemingly intentional;
therefore, upon seeing a great river, one must observe it."
